documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 1: Hydrogen Atom and Hydrogen Molecule
problems.statement:
![](p1-fig1)

Johann Jakob Balmer, a Swiss teacher, first expressed hydrogen's observed line-spectrum wavelengths as a series:

$$\frac1\lambda=R_H\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{n^2}\right),\qquad n=3,4,5,\ldots$$

Here the Rydberg constant is $R_H=m_ee^4/(8\varepsilon_0^2h^3c)=109678\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and $m_e$ is the electron mass. Bohr derived this expression in 1913; it generalizes to any one-electron atom or ion.

parts.statement: Calculate the longest wavelength in Å ($1\,\text{Å}=10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$) in the “Balmer series” of singly ionized helium, $\mathrm{He^+}$. Ignore nuclear motion.

Write the analogous formula for spectral transitions from higher levels to the lowest hydrogen-atom energy level. Use it to determine hydrogen's ground-state energy in eV.

A muonic hydrogen atom replaces the electron with a muon, about 207 times heavier but with the same charge. Ignore the muon's short lifetime.

Determine its lowest energy and first Bohr-orbit radius, ignoring nuclear motion. Hydrogen's Bohr radius is $a_0=\varepsilon_0h^2/(\pi m_ee^2)=0.53\,\text{Å}$.

Quantum mechanics replaces a classical orbit with an orbital. Hydrogen's ground-state orbital is

$$\Psi_{1s}(r)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi a_0^3}}e^{-r/a_0},$$

where $r$ is electron–nucleus distance.
Estimate the probability of finding the electron in a spherical shell of radius $a_0$ and thickness $0.001a_0$. A thin shell of inner radius $r$ has volume $4\pi r^2\Delta r$.

sections.title: Molecular dissociation
sections.statement:
Hydrogen dissociates through two channels:

$$\text{(i)}\quad\mathrm{H_2\to H+H},\qquad\text{(ii)}\quad\mathrm{H_2\to H^++H^-}.$$

The schematic energy–internuclear-distance diagram uses the same scale for atomic and molecular energies.

![](p1-fig2)

parts.statement: Put the appropriate channel labels (i) and (ii) in the boxes.
Determine the dissociation energies $D_e$ in eV for channels (i) and (ii).
From the data calculate the energy change for $\mathrm{H^-\to H+e^-}$.
$\mathrm{H^-}$ is a two-electron atom. Assuming Bohr's energy formula applies separately to each electron with nuclear charge $Z$ replaced by $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$, calculate $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

sections.statement:
The longest wavelength corresponds to $n=3$. For helium:

$$\frac1\lambda=4R_H\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{n^2}\right),\qquad\lambda_L=1641.1\,\text{Å}.$$

problems.title: Problem 2: Phosphoric Acid
problems.statement: Phosphoric acid is important to fertilizer production; it and its salts are also used in metal treatment, foods, detergents and toothpaste.

parts.statement:
At $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, successive dissociation constants have $pK_{1a}=2.12$, $pK_{2a}=7.21$, $pK_{3a}=12.32$. Write the conjugate base of dihydrogen phosphate and determine its $pK_b$.

Phosphoric acid adds sour or tart flavour to colas and root beers. A cola of density $1.00\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ contains 0.05% phosphoric acid by mass.
Determine the cola's pH, ignoring the second and third dissociation steps and assuming all acidity comes from phosphoric acid.

Add $1.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$ phosphoric acid to an aqueous soil suspension; its pH is 7.00. Determine fractional concentrations of all phosphate species, assuming no soil component interacts with them.

Plants absorb zinc, an essential micronutrient, only in water-soluble form. In soil water at pH 7.0, zinc phosphate is the only zinc and phosphate source. Calculate $[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]$ and $[\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}]$. Zinc phosphate has $K_{sp}=9.1\times10^{-33}$.

sections.statement:
The phosphoric-acid concentration is $0.5/98=0.0051\,\mathrm{M}$. For $\mathrm{H_3PO_4+H_2O\rightleftharpoons H_2PO_4^-+H_3O^+}$ the equilibrium concentrations are $0.0051-x$, $x$, $x$.

$pK_{1a}=2.12$ gives $K_{1a}=7.59\times10^{-3}$:

$$7.59\times10^{-3}=\frac{[\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{[\mathrm{H_3PO_4}]}=\frac{x^2}{0.0051-x}.$$

$x=[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]=3.49\times10^{-3}$; pH $=2.46$.

Let $X=\mathrm{PO_4}$ and $C$ be the total initial $\mathrm{H_3X}$ concentration:

$$f_0=\frac{[\mathrm{H_3X}]}C,\quad f_1=\frac{[\mathrm{H_2X^-}]}C,\quad f_2=\frac{[\mathrm{HX^{2-}}]}C,\quad f_3=\frac{[\mathrm{X^{3-}}]}C,\qquad f_0+f_1+f_2+f_3=1.$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
K_{1a}&=\frac{[\mathrm{H_2X^-}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{[\mathrm{H_3X}]}=\frac{f_1[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{f_0},\\
K_{2a}&=\frac{[\mathrm{HX^{2-}}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{[\mathrm{H_2X^-}]}=\frac{f_2[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{f_1},\\
K_{3a}&=\frac{[\mathrm{X^{3-}}][\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{[\mathrm{HX^{2-}}]}=\frac{f_3[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{f_2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

These give

$$f_0=\frac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]^3}{D},\quad f_1=\frac{K_{1a}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]^2}{D},\quad f_2=\frac{K_{1a}K_{2a}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]}{D},\quad f_3=\frac{K_{1a}K_{2a}K_{3a}}{D},$$

$$D=K_{1a}K_{2a}K_{3a}+K_{1a}K_{2a}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]+K_{1a}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]^2+[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]^3.$$

$K_{1a}=7.59\times10^{-3}$, $K_{2a}=6.17\times10^{-8}$, $K_{3a}=4.79\times10^{-13}$, and $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]=10^{-7}$ give

| Species | Fraction |
|---|---:|
| $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$ | $8.10\times10^{-6}$ |
| $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}$ | 0.618 |
| $\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}$ | 0.382 |
| $\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}$ | $1.83\times10^{-6}$ |

Let $S$ in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ be zinc-phosphate solubility. $[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]=3S$, total phosphate concentration $=2S$, and $[\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}]=f_3(2S)$. At pH 7, part 2.3 gives $f_3=1.83\times10^{-6}$.

$$K_{sp}=[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]^3[\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}]^2,\qquad9.1\times10^{-33}=(3S)^3(f_3\times2S)^2.$$

$[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]=9\times10^{-5}$; $[\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}]=1.1\times10^{-10}$; $S=3.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

problems.title: Problem 3: Second Law of Thermodynamics
problems.statement:
The second law of thermodynamics is a fundamental law of science. In this problem we consider the thermodynamics of an ideal gas, phase transitions and chemical equilibrium.

![](p3-fig1)

$3.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ expands isothermally, in thermal contact with its surroundings at $15\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, against fixed external pressure $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$. Initial and final volumes are 10.0 and $30.0\,\mathrm{dm^3}$.

parts.statement:
Mark the correct option for system and surroundings entropy changes:

- ☐ (a) $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}>0$, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sur}}=0$.
- ☐ (b) $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}<0$, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sur}}>0$.
- ☐ (c) $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}>0$, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sur}}<0$.
- ☐ (d) Both zero.
Calculate $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}$, treating carbon dioxide as ideal.
Calculate $\Delta S_{\mathrm{sur}}$.
Calculate the universe's entropy change. Does it agree with the second law? Mark yes or no.

sections.title: Phase transitions
sections.statement:
The schematic pressure–temperature diagram is not to scale.

![](p3-fig2)

parts.statement: Cool carbon dioxide from 4.0 bar and $10.0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at constant pressure. Choose: (a) first liquid then solid; (b) directly solid without liquid.
Compress carbon dioxide isothermally from the same initial conditions. Choose: (a) first liquid then solid; (b) directly solid without liquid.
Use the phase-diagram data to calculate the molar sublimation enthalpy. Write the formula used.

Carbon monoxide, widely used in organic synthesis, can be made by reacting carbon dioxide with graphite. Show that the equilibrium constant at 298.15 K is less than unity using these data:

| Species | $\Delta_fH^{\circ}$ / $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ | $S^{\circ}$ / $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| $\mathrm{CO_2(g)}$ | −393.51 | 213.79 |
| $\mathrm{CO(g)}$ | −110.53 | 197.66 |
| C(graphite) | — | 5.74 |
Estimate the temperature at which this reaction's equilibrium constant equals 1, ignoring slight thermodynamic-data variations with temperature.
React carbon dioxide with excess hot graphite at about $800\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and total pressure 5.0 bar. $K_p=10.0$. Calculate equilibrium carbon-monoxide partial pressure.

sections.statement:
Entropy is path-independent, so use isothermal reversible ideal-gas expansion:

$$\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}=nR\ln(V_f/V_i)=27.4\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}.$$
$\Delta S_{\mathrm{uni}}=\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}}+\Delta S_{\mathrm{sur}}=20.5\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Yes, this agrees with the second law.

$\Delta H^{\circ}=172.45\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta S^{\circ}=176\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$, $\Delta G^{\circ}=\Delta H^{\circ}-T\Delta S^{\circ}=120\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. A positive $\Delta G^{\circ}$ implies $K<1$.

For $\mathrm{CO_2(g)+C(s)\rightleftharpoons2CO(g)}$ the printed amounts are $1-\alpha$ and $2\alpha$. The printed partial-pressure expressions are

$$p(\mathrm{CO_2})=\frac{1-\alpha}{1-\alpha}\times5,\qquad p(\mathrm{CO})=\frac{2\alpha}{1-\alpha}\times5,$$

$$K_p=\frac{p(\mathrm{CO})^2}{p(\mathrm{CO_2})},\qquad p(\mathrm{CO})=3.7\,\mathrm{bar}.$$

problems.title: Problem 4: Beach Sand Mineral Monazite (descriptive title)
problems.statement:
![](p4-fig1)

Monazite, a beach-sand mineral abundant in Kerala, India, is rich in thorium. A typical sample contains about 9% $\mathrm{ThO_2}$ and 0.35% $\mathrm{U_3O_8}$. $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$ and $^{206}\mathrm{Pb}$ are stable end products of $^{232}\mathrm{Th}$ and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ decay, respectively. All lead in monazite is radiogenic.

Mass spectrometry gives isotopic atom ratio $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}/{}^{232}\mathrm{Th}=0.104$. The half-lives of $^{232}\mathrm{Th}$ and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ are $1.41\times10^{10}$ and $4.47\times10^9$ years, respectively. Assume all four isotopes remained entirely in the sample since formation.

parts.statement: Calculate the sample's age, the elapsed time since formation.
Estimate the $^{206}\mathrm{Pb}/{}^{238}\mathrm{U}$ isotopic atom ratio.

Thorium-232 is a fertile nuclear-energy material. Under thermal neutron irradiation it absorbs a neutron, and the resulting isotope forms $^{233}\mathrm{U}$ through successive $\beta^-$ decays. Write these nuclear reactions.

sections.title: Sequential fission-product decay
sections.statement:
Uranium-233 fission produces a complex radioactive mixture. Molybdenum-101 initially decays as

$$^{101}_{42}\mathrm{Mo}\xrightarrow{t_{1/2}=14.6\,\mathrm{min}}{}^{101}_{43}\mathrm{Tc}\xrightarrow{t_{1/2}=14.3\,\mathrm{min}}{}^{101}_{44}\mathrm{Ru}.$$

parts.statement: A freshly prepared radiochemically pure sample initially contains 5000 atoms of $^{101}\mathrm{Mo}$. After 14.6 min, how many atoms of (i) $^{101}\mathrm{Mo}$, (ii) $^{101}\mathrm{Tc}$ and (iii) $^{101}\mathrm{Ru}$ are present?

sections.statement:
$$N=N_0e^{-0.6931t/t_{1/2}},\qquad\frac{N_0-N}{N}=e^{+0.6931t/t_{1/2}}-1.$$

$N_0-N$ is the number of thorium atoms decayed, equal to the lead-208 atoms formed. Thus $(N_0-N)/N=0.104$ and

$$e^{0.6931t/(1.41\times10^{10})}=1.104,\qquad t=2.01\times10^9\text{ years}.$$

Let $x$ be the required ratio:

$$x=e^{+0.6931t/t_{1/2}}-1.$$

Using $t=2.01\times10^9$ years and $t_{1/2}=4.47\times10^9$ years gives $x=0.366$.

(i) After one half-life, $N_1=2500$ molybdenum atoms.

(ii) The technetium population is

$$N_2=\frac{N_0\lambda_1}{\lambda_2-\lambda_1}(e^{-\lambda_1t}-e^{-\lambda_2t}),$$

where $N_0=5000$, $\lambda_1=(0.693/14.6)\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and $\lambda_2=(0.693/14.3)\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$. At 14.6 min, $N_2=1710$.

(iii) $N_3=N_0-N_1-N_2=790$ ruthenium atoms.

problems.title: Problem 5: Halogen Chemistry
problems.statement: Halogens react among themselves and with many other elements, forming compounds with diverse structures, bonding and chemical behaviour. Metal halides, halogen derivatives and interhalogens are major types.

sections.title: (A) Photography
sections.statement: A black-and-white photographic film has a silver-bromide coating on a support such as cellulose acetate.

parts.statement: Write the photochemical reaction when light falls on $\mathrm{AgBr(s)}$ on a film.
During developing, sodium thiosulphate washes away unexposed AgBr by complexing Ag(I). Write this reaction.
Metallic silver can be recovered from the waste washings by adding cyanide and then zinc. Write the reactions.

sections.title: (B) Shapes, spectra and reactivity
sections.statement: Fluorine, the most reactive halogen, reacts under controlled conditions with $\mathrm{Cl_2}$, $\mathrm{Br_2}$ and $\mathrm{I_2}$ to give tetra-atomic, hexa-atomic and octa-atomic molecules, respectively.

parts.statement:
Write their formulas and three-dimensional VSEPR structures. Show the central atom's lone pairs where appropriate.

Iodine vapour mixed with chlorine in a mass spectrometer gives molecular-ion peak sets A and B:

- A: $m/z=162,164$.
- B: $m/z=464,466,468,470,472,474,476$.

Identify the species at $m/z=162,164,466,476$, showing each isotopic composition. Draw the heaviest ($m/z=476$), clearly indicating lone pairs on iodine atoms.

In water, chlorine oxidizes sodium thiosulphate to an ion with sulphur's highest oxidation state.
Write the reaction equation.
Write thiosulphate's Lewis-dot structure. Circle the sulphur atom with the lower oxidation state.
Chlorine dioxide reacts with sodium hydroxide “as shown below”. Identify chlorine-containing products X and Y and balance the equation.
Chlorine reacting with an alkali is used to manufacture bleach. Write the formation reaction.
Write chlorine's oxidation state or states in bleach.

sections.title: (C) Alkali metal halides and X-ray crystallography
sections.statement:
X-ray crystallography reveals metal-halide structures. The radius ratio $r_+/r_-$ helps rationalize structure and stability. The native graph schematically relates NaCl- and CsCl-type structure energies to radius ratio, keeping $r_-$ constant.

| Anion / cation | $\mathrm{Li^+}$ | $\mathrm{Na^+}$ | $\mathrm{K^+}$ | $\mathrm{Rb^+}$ | $\mathrm{Cs^+}$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ | 0.33 | 0.52 | 0.74 | 0.82 | 0.93 |
| $\mathrm{Br^-}$ | 0.31 | 0.49 | 0.68 | 0.76 | 0.87 |
| $\mathrm{I^-}$ | 0.28 | 0.44 | 0.62 | 0.69 | 0.78 |

parts.statement: For a given anion, why does the NaCl-type graph level off at low $r_+/r_-$? Mark: (a) cation–cation contact along a face diagonal; (b) anion–anion contact along a face diagonal; (c) cation–anion contact along a cell edge.
Which of LiBr, NaBr and RbBr is likely to change from NaCl-type to CsCl-type with temperature and/or pressure?
Calculate the radius ratio where the CsCl-type energy levels off.

With CuKα X-rays ($\lambda=154\,\mathrm{nm}$, as printed), KCl (fcc) diffracts at $\theta=14.2^{\circ}$. Given $h^2+k^2+l^2=4$, $d_{hkl}=a/\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}$ in a cubic crystal, and fcc reflections requiring all-odd or all-even Miller indices, calculate lattice parameter $a$.

Complete the table for the second and third nearest neighbours of a potassium ion:

| Quantity | Second nearest neighbours | Third nearest neighbours |
|---|---|---|
| Number | ______ | ______ |
| Charge sign | ______ | ______ |
| Distance / pm | ______ | ______ |
Determine the lowest possible diffraction angle for KCl.
